#1328. What's wrong with Erling Haaland? Man City's superstar has been radiating an air of gloom in front of the cameras - but it's his form on the pitch that should most concern Enzo Maresca, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 08:22 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:10 EST, 25 November 2026

A smile did eventually spread across the face of Erling Haaland when dissecting Manchester City’s draw with Napoli, stretching their worrying run to one victory in five games.

Not for the first time in recent weeks, he had appeared morose and despondent, radiating an air of gloom, talking about how the team are ‘questioning anything’ amid these results. That’s not exactly inspiring confidence among their supporters.

But just as City’s captain for the night was about to finish his media duties before heading home, one final question focused on Sunday’s clash with Arsenal and a rivalry with a ‘certain centre half’. Haaland’s mood changed instantly.

‘It's always good to play against the best teams,’ said the Norwegian, breaking out into a smirk as he allowed the impending battle with Gabriel to percolate.

‘Arsenal were the best team last year and one of the best in the last five years now, so it's fun to play against them and it’s always fun to play against Gabriel.’

There was, at last, some positive emotion. Is Gabriel and that playground scrapping what he needs to re-energise? We’ll find out in a few days.

Erling Haaland appeared morose and despondent following Man City's draw with Napoli, suggesting he was 'questioning everything' amid their worrying run of form

Haaland did raise a smile about the prospect of his impending battle with Arsenal defender Gabriel this weekend

The Man City star has shown increasing dejected body language during games and has spent too much time recently with his head bowed and hand waving at team-mates

Haaland talked about City needing to be at their maximum to take anything from the Emirates this weekend. Whether that is ‘fun’ or not is a different matter entirely, but what Enzo Maresca must demand more from all of his players. Even with 14 goals already this term, that includes Haaland.

He is leading from the front off the pitch. Standing in front of the cameras more than anyone else, facing up to the dipping form and taking on those responsibilities without complaining. The forward wrote on X on Wednesday afternoon: 'Together through the ups and downs. Thank you for pushing us until the very end yesterday. Full focus on Sunday now.'

Yet City need more of that leadership between the white lines from somebody who has drawn a blank in four of his last five club matches, despite scoring three times over the international break.

There is too much head bowing and hand waving at the moment.

The 26-year-old admits he has to give extra. And believes that the team are generally creating enough chances for him, even if the freewheeling attacking abandon of early season has vanished.

City's results are clearly affecting Haaland’s mood and that can be self-perpetuating. He admits that failing to reverse this run is hurting him. That is evident by watching his increasingly dejected body language during games and the frustration seen when he gestured at Abdukodir Khusanov as the defender dithered with a routine throw-in during Saturday’s draw against Fulham. It wasn’t the picture of a man happy with his lot.

Only Haaland will know whether that general angst is contributing to a lack of intensity in his own performances. Nobody has mentioned the striker carrying a knock, although Maresca has appeared focused on offering him rest whenever possible over the past three months.

Something is undoubtedly proving an obstacle for him. He’s insisted that it isn’t the guilty verdicts hanging over City and, listening to him, the gripes and disappointment look focused on City’s lack of control in games. It also cannot help that Haaland will feel aggrieved to have seen a goal on Saturday chalked off for a foul on Bernd Leno and then to have not been awarded a penalty for grappling on Tuesday night.

If both or even one of those decisions go his way, the interview that sparked concern with fans – one conducted almost immediately after full time when emotions are at their highest – would likely have been very different.

City will have to cling on to the idea that a sullen Haaland is at least a Haaland who cares. And a Haaland who cares must surely dig them out of this hole, even if he cannot do that alone.

After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

#1326. Celtic's European opponents are plankton in football's great ocean... but Portuguese second-tier strugglers Torreense have already made waves in Europe this season

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 12:29 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:33 EST, 25 November 2026

Even for aficionados of the continental game, the draw for the Europa League this year was likely to cause a degree of puzzlement.

While not the only outfit to be making its debut in one of UEFA’s competitions, the name of S.C.U. Torreense rang precious few bells among supporters of clubs with a vested interest in how the cards might fall. And little wonder.

The Portuguese side are plankton in football’s great ocean. Not only have they never played on this stage before, they haven’t even come close to it.

An extraordinary triumph in the Portuguese Cup final – the Taca de Portugal – against Sporting Lisbon in May was their ticket to this journey. In all likelihood, this European adventure will be their first and their last.

It is, of course, not the done thing for anyone connected with any particular club to express a preference as to who they might be drawn against. But representatives of any one of the 35 other sides present at the Grimaldi Forum in Monaco in late August who claimed they weren’t privately hoping for a match against the men from the small city of Torres Vedras were lying.

Never mind Benfica, Porto and Sporting Lisbon, the traditional footballing powerhouses of that nation. In terms of support, stature and history, this outfit are a world removed from the likes of Braga and Vitoria Guimaraes, the perennial challengers to the big three.

Torreense players celebrate their victory over Armenian side Ararat in their last European tie

Torreense’s place in the food chain is underscored by the fact that they can’t even play European matches in their 2,400-capacity Estadio Manuel Marques home because it doesn’t match UEFA criteria.

For the purposes of the Europa League, their fans, who primarily hail from a place which sits 25 miles north of Lisbon, will have to travel to Leiria, which is 60 miles north of their home.

Those looking to pick up a late ticket for the visit of Celtic should have no concerns. Built for Euro 2004, the Estadio Municipal de Leiria holds 23,888 spectators. Torreense, who were a tier three side as recently as 2022, draw an average crowd of around 1,300.

The fact is that it’s not only a second division Portuguese side which Martin O’Neill’s men will face on matchday five. It’s a struggling one.

After ten matches in Liga Portugal 2, Joao Nuno’s men lie 13th of 18, 31st place overall in Portugal. They’ve won just twice this season, against Amarante and Benfica B, and have already had their cup defence ended by Benfica’s big boys.

Nuno was only appointed at the end of October after Luis Tralhao, who lifted the only major honour in the club’s history, was fired after a dismal start.

Portuguese coach Joao Nuno only took charge at the struggling second-tier side this season

Yet the concern for O’Neill and his players is that the Torreense which routinely fails to impress in its domestic division bears little resemblance to the one which has so far pitched up on its maiden European adventure.

In one of the most eye-catching results of the opening night, the Portuguese minnows travelled to Norway and defeated Lillestrom, a respected name throughout Europe, 2-1.

Sunderland were the first visitors to Leiria in October. What a game Torreense gave the Premier League side, leading by a goal only to narrowly lose the match late on.

While a 4-1 loss to Celtic’s old foes Ferencvaros in Budapest was something of a reality check, Nuno’s players fought back from a goal down to beat Ararat-Armenia in injury time last time out at their adopted home.

So, despite being wretched in their own league, they have six points in the Europa League and presently sit in 19th place, above the likes of Real Sociedad, AC Milan and Marseille.

With nine points possibly being enough to squeeze through to the play-off round, a famous win against Celtic could do the trick with three games to spare. With around £400,000 earned in prize money for any victory, you’d better believe they’ll be up for this.

Having just about lived to tell the tale last month, Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris gave Celtic a warning about what lies in store on Thursday.

Despite their lowly status, Torreense are above AC Milan, Celtic and Marseille in the table

‘It’s a good team they know how to manage this kind of game,’ said the Frenchman. ‘They’re well organised and hard to break down with this deep block. They try to seize every opportunity.’

A limited side which sits in and plays with caution? Those Celtic supporters who had the misfortune to watch their favourites fail to break down an atrocious Kairat Almaty outfit across 210 minutes little over a year ago will be rightly concerned.

While the Parkhead men’s poor record on the road across many years includes some thumpings at the hands of super clubs including Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain, there have been enough stumbles against lesser sides to ensure nothing can be taken for granted.

O’Neill will point to the displays in last season’s victories away to Feyenoord and Stuttgart as examples of what he’s looking for. While not on his watch, the catastrophe away to Kairat remains a useful illustration of what may happen if the players aren’t at it.

With an early goal likely to kick the legs from under Torreense, Celtic cannot allow them to feel comfortable in their shape.

In order to disrupt the Portuguese, it will be a night for the visitors to play with speed and imagination. To get in behind their defence, O’Neill’s wingers need to shine.

Sunderland required a late goal from Noah Sadiki to emerge with a victory on their trip to Leiria

This will have informed the veteran’s thinking as he sought to draft in a replacement for the injured Mika Baur.

While bringing in Joel van den Berg would have made sense from a positional point of view, Jota has started to show signs that he’s moving through the levels after a year-and-a-half out injured. A goal or an assist on his return to his homeland would allow the former Benfica man to underscore that point.

A constant threat against St Mirren, Yang Hyun-jun should start on the right flank ahead of Haissem Hassan. Together with Seb Tounekti, the Egyptian increasingly feels like a peripheral player.

Even if Benjamin Nygren is available again after a heel injury, O’Neill will be loath to drop Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain or Luke McCowan after both showed up well when played alongside Callum McGregor in the weekend win.

The issue of Kasper Hogh’s 16-game goal drought will only become pertinent if the free-scoring Camilo Duran can first help to put the game to bed.

Fit-again winger Jota could feature for Celtic on his return to Portuguese soil

Celtic badly need this to be a rare straightforward evening on the road in Europe. Goodness knows, they’ve had precious few of those in recent times.

A win to go with the one they claimed last time out against Besiktas would leave them in a decent position in the competition, with a further four points from their remaining matches with Omonia, Marseille and Union Saint-Gilloise then assuring them of progression.

Anything other than that outcome tonight doesn’t bear thinking about. Almost 60 years on from Jock Stein’s side becoming sporting immortals by defeating Inter Milan in Lisbon, their successors must tick a box and ensure tiny Torreense’s reputation in the game remains as lowly as it has ever been.

#1325. Inside Raheem Sterling's rise from childhood tragedy and poverty to England superstar at the peak of his powers - but Lamborghini crash and laughing gas addiction leave him staring into the abyss

Published: 08:02 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 13:10 EST, 25 November 2026

In September, shortly after pleading guilty to dangerous driving and drug possession, Raheem Sterling shared a statement on social media.

The goal, he implied with a picture of graffiti on a wall, was to 'be better than yesterday' and the intention was to seek 'progress over perfection', as he captioned the image.

But for the former England and Manchester City star to move forward, he has had to fall a long way.

The 31-year-old avoided prison, but was handed a 12-month suspended sentence and 100 hours of community service at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court after he was involved in a dangerous crash in May. Sterling had been driving his £270,000 Lamborghini Urus SUV while under the influence of laughing gas, with multiple motorists spotting him using balloons at the wheel while careening down the M25 and M3 motorways.

During his sentencing hearing, Sterling revealed that he has undergone a 12-day stint in rehab soon after the arrest, after contacting UK addiction services.

The number of footballers in history who have found themselves entangled with the British justice system is not a small one. But against the backdrop of Sterling's personal story, his fall is a particularly poignant one. The former international built a remarkable career out of a difficult upbringing.

Raheem Sterling has been handed a suspended sentence and 100 hours of community service after being convicted of dangerous driving

The former Manchester City star has experienced some of the highest heights in professional football - but now languishes without a club

Sterling lost his father at the age of just two to gun violence, prompting his mother's move from his birthplace of Kingston, Jamaica to the London suburb of Neasden.

Speaking to the Players' Tribune in 2018, Sterling admitted that the tragedy had 'shaped his entire life'.

'For a few years, we lived with our grandmother in Kingston, and I remember watching the other kids with their mums and just feeling really jealous,' he revealed. 'I didn't fully understand what my mum was doing for us. I just knew that she was gone. My grandma was amazing, but everybody wants their mum at that age.'

His father's shocking death also inspired a gun tattoo inked on his leg above his right 'shooting' foot, there as part of a promise he had made that he 'would never touch a gun in his lifetime'. Although the tattoo prompted criticism from anti-gun campaigners in 2018, Sterling was adamant that his message was aligned with theirs, with the player backed by the FA.

After moving to England, his mother Nadine found work as a cleaner. Sterling and his siblings would sometimes help her during her early morning shifts cleaning hotels at 5am before their school day started. With rent a continual challenge for the family as money was tight, they moved house often.

But Sterling's prodigious talent on the football pitch was breaking through, with the winger asked to join Queens Park Rangers' youth set-up at just 10 years old.

Sacrifices were made to allow for this: in 2021, Sterling released a custom football boot with New Balance paying tribute to the three buses - the 18, the 182 and 140 - he had to catch to make the return journey from home near Wembley to the west London training ground, accompanied by his older sister Lakima.

'The red double-deckers with the blue wool '80s vibe on the seats,' he reminisced. 'Spent ages on those. We'd leave at 3.15 and get home at 11 pm. Every. Single. Day.

'She'd sit upstairs in the little cafe and chill until I was done with training. Imagine being 17 years old and doing that for your little brother. And I never once heard her say, 'Nah, I don't wanna take him.'

As a youngster, Sterling's footballing talent was prodigious and helped him sign with QPR at the age of 10

Five years later and Sterling had parlayed this into a move to Liverpool's academy, with the star breaking through to the first team in 2012

'At the time, I didn't understand how much she was sacrificing. Her and my mum got me here. My whole family played a massive part in my life. Without them, you wouldn't even know me.'

Football was a necessary focus as well as passion, with Sterling once removed from mainstream education as a youngster and sent to Vernon House, an adapted school to help with behavioral problems.

His teacher there, Chris Beschi, told the Guardian in 2018 that he had said to a young Sterling: 'If you carry on the way you're going, by the time you're 17 you'll either be playing for England or you'll be in prison.'

But Beschi was able to see a different side to Sterling too, describing the boy as having 'a kind and innocent passion about him', and as football took over, Premier League rivals clamoured to sign him up to their youth ranks.

Nadine was adamant that he should be developed outside of London to avoid any possibility of getting caught up in gang violence, and Chelsea and Arsenal's loss was Liverpool's gain, with Sterling joining the academy at the age of 15 for a then punchy fee of £500,000.

After that, Sterling's career quickly gathered momentum. With the arrival of Liverpool legend Kenny Dalglish in the dugout in early 2011, Sterling was moved into the Europa League squad, fast-tracking integration with established first-team stars. Playing and travel time was limited, however.

Just over a year later, and the player was readied for his first senior start against Wigan Athletic, at the tender age of 17 years and 107 days. The following season saw him named as the club's Young Player of the Year and shortlisted for the PFA Young Player of the Year. By 2014, he was winning the Golden Boy award, and becoming the most expensive English footballer to date with his £49million move to Man City.

But against the backdrop of success on the football pitch, there were challenging moments away from it. In 2013, Sterling was accused of two separate counts of assault, one against a former girlfriend and another against a different woman. He was found not guilty of the former, with the latter incident dropped after a witness failed to attend court.

Two years later, in March 2015, Sterling was snapped by tabloids reportedly smoking from a shisha pipe. And, in a moment that spoke of what was to come, it was alleged that he might have also been using nitrous oxide for recreational purposes. Manager Brendan Rodgers was keen to protect Sterling and urged people to remember: 'Young players make mistakes.'

Sterling had an uneven stint at Liverpool but put on display enough of his talent to earn him the 2014 Golden Boy award

His spell on Merseyside also secured him entrance into the England squad, where he became one of the standouts of the 2010s

Shortly before his move to Man City Sterling started dating Paige Milian, now his long-term partner and mother of his children (Source: Instagram/Raheem Sterling)

The clean slate offered by Man City might have itself been appealing. Things had become somewhat tricky at Anfield, after Sterling had refused a new deal, with the player booed while on duty for England under then-manager Roy Hodgson. Rodgers and Sterling rowed publicly in the media over suggestions that he had turned down a new contract for financial reasons, and his move to the Etihad came after club legends including Steven Gerrard, Jamie Carragher and Graeme Souness had all criticised his conduct.

The first season at the Etihad might have been a false start, with Sterling notably injured in March leading to the premature curtailing of his campaign, but under incoming manager Pep Guardiola, Sterling began flying. At the same time, he was underscoring his importance for England under Hodgson, and then Gareth Southgate.

'In terms of, "Can he fulfil it?", he'll give himself every chance,' Southgate said when asked if he thought Sterling might win the Ballon d'Or after victory against Kosovo in 2019. 'There are some outstanding players around - (Eden) Hazard, (Kevin) De Bruyne, Messi, Ronaldo.

'But he (Sterling) has got the drive, he's got the professionalism, he's got the ability. He's physically and mentally strong for such a small-statured lad.'

And against the backdrop of his growth on the pitch, Sterling was becoming an important voice away from it too, frequently speaking out against the racism young black players were targeted with, and from personal experience. In 2017, Sterling was attacked outside Man City's training ground by a convicted football hooligan hurling racist language at him. In 2018, he suffered racist abuse on the pitch while featuring for Man City against Chelsea.

396 Premier League appearances, 123 goals

GQ magazine described Sterling as football's 'most influential player' in 2019 in recognition of his climb to the very top of the game, and for his increasingly high profile as a campaigner off the pitch.

Sterling branded negative tabloid coverage as racist, and made an address to the United Nations.

'Discrimination is discrimination. It doesn't matter if it's your sexuality, or your color, you shouldn't (discriminate) at all', Sterling said, speaking to the UN Human Rights Office for the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. 'We need – as a collective – to take responsibility. This is a new age where color can't define who you are'.

Sterling also established the Raheem Sterling Foundation in 2021, which the footballer funds and which helps to support youth education projects, including fighting knife crime and helping children out of poverty. That year, he was awarded an MBE for services to racial equality in sport.

As his public profile hit new heights, Sterling kept scoring, becoming Man City's seventh-highest goalscorer of all time. But limited game time under Guardiola led to a move to Chelsea for £47.5m, and on a salary worth an eye-watering £325,000 per week.

Sterling was a focal point of the Man City team which achieved a staggering trophy haul in the late 2010s

His move to Chelsea in 2022 set him up to be one of the stars of the club's new era under BlueCo but he failed to hit the right notes across two personally underwhelming seasons

After an abortive loan move to Arsenal, Sterling signed for Feyenoord at the start of the year but did not see his deal extended past the end of the season

In what might be seen as the beginning of the end, his first season in Chelsea blue failed to hit the heights required. There was chaos in west London as the club cycled through Thomas Tuchel, Graham Potter, Bruno Saltor and Frank Lampard in the dugout but Sterling still bagged nine goals and a further four assists in his 38 appearances, as well as securing a place in Southgate's World Cup squad that year.

Sterling made an impact in the group stages in Qatar, but was forced home after his family home was burgled. While his long-term partner Paige Milian and three children were not at the property, Sterling was shaken and flew back to Oxshott from the camp before returning in time for the quarter-final against France.

While his first season with Chelsea had room for improvement at Stamford Bridge, his second was even limper. The latest manager on the club's merry-go-round, Enzo Maresca, said in August 2024 that he was going to 'struggle' for minutes, effectively frozen out.

From there, his on-pitch decline was swift. An abortive loan across the city to Arsenal had the promise of a step up, but Sterling struggled just as hard for game time. A difficult time was compounded by a second break-in at his home, with the family forced to escape but luckily unharmed.

On his return to Chelsea, Maresca placed him in the now-infamous bomb squad, forced to train away from the first-team players, share separate, smaller locker rooms, and all but ostracised within Cobham.

Offers swirled around Sterling as they have done for all his decorated career, but the possibility of a move to Bayer Leverkusen or Juventus did not go much further than exploratory talks. A switch to nearby Fulham fell through. With money far from a motivating factor, the winger opted not to accept a lucrative contract and move to Saudi Arabia.

Instead, Sterling stayed out of the game until his contract was mutually terminated in January of this year.

Hopes of finding that at his next club Feyenoord evaporated on his debut. Signed until the end of the 2025-26 season, Sterling stepped onto the pitch in February after nine months out and looked rusty.

The critics were brutal, but head coach Robin van Persie did his best to defend his new player. It was too harsh to judge him over just six or eight weeks, he stressed.

Within weeks, he was back in the UK, with his arrest coming in May. Any offers that might have come his way over the summer have subsequently dried up.

Sterling crashed his £270,000 Lambourghini Urus while driving under the influence

The arrest took place shortly after his time in Rotterdam came to an end, with the star pleading guilty in September

Since the arrest, Sterling has been keeping a low profile and focusing on his family (Source: Instagram/Raheem Sterling)

With offers from football clubs quieter, the winger has focused on other ventures including his Playmaker Films (Source: Instagram/Raheem Sterling)

Sterling has since worked on his Playmaker Films, a content agency, and launched 'The Cage', a grassroots football competition where teams of four face off for eight minutes with £5,000 on the line.

'Football's about expressing yourself,' he said when interviewed about why he created the contest, which showcases individuality on caged pitches similar to ones he would have learned to play on. 'The game is a beautiful thing'.

Sterling's story is of a remarkable rise from adversity to the highest levels in professional sport. His private life has clearly been complicated - District Judge Kirsty Allman revealed his drug problem had 'become a maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period in his career'.

#1324. Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy

A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Pressed on whether Fernandes’s comments were all the more insidious and divisive at a time when the manager was trying to pull the squad together so soon after Martínez’s outburst, Carrick added: “Yeah, the most important thing for me is the team.

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”

Carrick, Wilcox and United chief executive Omar Berrada held a meeting with Martínez in the wake of his criticism but the manager would not be drawn on whether he had spoken with Fernandes and it remains to be seen if he will be captain or start against Bournemouth.

“If I’ve spoken to him or haven’t spoken to him, I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail,” he said.

Carrick agreed that United collectively needed to stop turning on each other in public. “We need to move forward in the right direction. We need to do things that enable us to do that. That’s pretty clear,” he said.

“It [the dressing room] is not divided, no. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

Separately, Carrick expressed sympathy for Fernandes over the “awful” burglary at his home on Wednesday night when he was in Italy, and said the club “are doing a lot of work to support Bruno and his family”.

Carrick is under huge pressure heading into Bournemouth but said he was happy to take the heat if it enabled his players to perform.

“It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, and what we are as a group, and what we look like, and what we feel like,” he said. “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry.”

Nonetheless, Carrick admitted he was “hurting an awful lot” and that the team had to get back to showing the values and qualities that have underpinned the club’s historic success after a “really unacceptable” performance against Como and wider struggles. United have won two of 11 matches this season.

“I’m not entitled to be here,” Carrick said. “We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.

“I’m fully aware of that. It takes hard work, a lot of sacrifice. You’ve got to invest yourself in the club and you’ve got to do a lot of things that maybe aren’t so nice, but you’ve got to do it for each other, and you’ve got to win.

“It’s important we live up to that, and it’s important for me to push those values, and for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

“We’ve kind of lost our way a bit if I’m honest, and we will get it back. I’m totally confident we’ll get it back. Respect this club, respect what it takes, because it’s very important to me.”

Carrick added that he was inspired by the values of “humility, hard work, resilience, sacrifice and pride” embodied by the likes of Busby, Ferguson, Charlton, Giggs and Rooney.

“We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that,” he said. “We’ve had it for a spell, I feel very strongly about that. It inspires me a lot to live up to that and keep driving that with the players.

“There’s a resilience about this club that’s been shown for a long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, success, sustaining success, there’s a resilience in this club that runs very deep.”

Carrick was trailed by a camera crew from Amazon Prime as he entered the media auditorium at Manchester United’s Carrington training base at 1.30pm on Friday.

There have been plenty of dark moments at Old Trafford in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era. But the difference this season is that any internal drama will soon be available for public consumption after the decision to allow cameras into a once-sacrosanct dressing room.

Whether Carrick will see out the next week, let alone a season being captured by filmmakers from Amazon’s All Or Nothing series, who probably cannot believe their luck at the unfolding crisis, remains to be seen. He certainly needs a big reaction against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at the very least.

But it became clear as he began his press conference with an emotional 5½-minute monologue that he would not go down without a fight.

#1323. Why Aberdeen's new gem Marshall will keep sparkling if Frick persists with diamond formation

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 13:00 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 13:13 EST, 25 November 2026

Nicky Devlin has predicted that Findlay Marshall will continue to sparkle if he’s played at the top of Aberdeen’s diamond formation.

On the back of netting his first senior goal for the Dons from the bench against Kilmarnock, new boss Mario Frick deployed the 20-year-old from the start against Rangers in a central attacking role.

In what proved to be a man of the match display, Marshall set up Brad Lyons’ opener then claimed a goal of his own with a sweet left-foot finish.

And with Frick seemingly intent on sticking with the blueprint which caused Killie and Rangers problems, defender Devlin believes his younger team-mate, who enjoyed a successful loan spell at Arbroath last season, will only go from strength to strength.

‘Even at Arbroath, you saw how much of a goal threat he is,’ said Devlin. ‘He makes really good runs into the box and off both feet he’s a really good finisher.

‘He can definitely play other roles, especially in the formation that the manager’s been playing just now. But I think you get the best out of him when you let him attack the box, let him get into the box to score goals.

‘For me, he was the best player on the park. Especially for someone so young, to go there... he’ll probably hate me for saying it, but I could tell he was maybe a wee bit nervous because he told me about three or four times that it’s the first time he’d ever been to Ibrox.

Findlay Marshall in the thick of the action against Rangers in this week's 3-2 loss for Dons

‘So, I knew he was thinking about it. But then he goes and delivers a performance like that.

‘His finishing, especially off his left foot, is unbelievable. He could easily have got us a draw. He was really unlucky with an effort right at the end.

‘He’s grown so much, especially since I came to the club at first. He’s an example for everyone at our club in terms of youth players. He’s gone and done what the club wanted him to do. He’s had two or three different loans where he’s gone away, played well, scored goals, came back, had to wait his opportunity.

‘In the last two games that he’s come in, he’s scored two goals and he’s been brilliant.’

Marshall’s first goal for the Dons at Rugby Park was another crisp left-foot finish which came when he decided not to play in a team-mate.

Devlin feels that the better decision-making he’s now showing is a sign that his game is starting to click into place.

‘He’s a younger boy who just wants to learn all the time,’ he explained. ‘He mentioned after the game on Saturday that he had a chance like that in the cup and he chose the other option. He tried to play in maybe the more senior player just because he thought that was the right thing to do. He took on board that he should have maybe gone himself.

‘It was an unbelievable finish. That’s what he brings to the team. That’s what he can bring to us. And hopefully he can keep doing that.’

Marshall is only 20 but was Aberdeen's star man in the match at Ibrox on Tuesday night

Born in Stonehaven and part of the Dons’ set-up since 2017, Marshall is the new poster boy for the club.

At a time when the opportunities being afforded to young Scots is a hot topic, Devlin feels that Aberdeen have much to feel optimistic about on that score.

‘I think we’ve got plenty here that I think can definitely step up and come in,’ he explained.

‘You see towards the end of the game, we’re chasing a goal with 20 minutes to go and the manager turns to a 15-year-old (Andrew Fasanya). So, there’s players there that can come through.

‘There’s a few boys out on loan now that are doing excellent. The two Alfies at Inverness (Bavidge and Stewart) and Dylan Lobban has done brilliant at Dunfermline.

‘So, there’s definitely players there that can step up for us. Hopefully, they’ll get their opportunity through time. But I’m pretty sure the manager’s trying to assess everyone in the squad just now.’

Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.

City’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He writes: “With Pep Guardiola and Jürgen Klopp having departed the Premier League, there can now be little doubt that Unai Emery is the best manager in England’s top division. And by some distance.

“Saturday will mark four years since Villa unveiled Emery as their head coach and few could have predicted the success that has followed. He has proved an inspired appointment who has continually embarrassed the “Big Six” clubs.

“On every level, he has delivered: points per game, net spend, a distinguishable style of play, improving individual players, over-performance in the league and European competition.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

However, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

Villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

Emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

#1321. Blend public cash and private innovation to unlock drug development

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Victor J. Dzau is a professor of medicine at Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA.

Will Ellaissi is head of product at Switchboard, MD, Atlanta, Georgia, USA.

Emily L. Shambaugh is special assistant and policy adviser at Duke University in Washington DC, USA.

A fresh model of research and development is needed to incentivize manufacturers to go after diseases that aren’t sure bets.Credit: Stanislav Gvozd/Getty

For decades, most countries have followed the same model of biomedical innovation. Basic research is undertaken mostly by universities and academia, and private industry leads the translation of research into health solutions1.

This approach has generated extraordinary drugs and therapies as well as economic success. In 2022, the pharmaceutical sector contributed US$2.3 trillion — or around 1.7% — to global gross domestic product (GDP) and supported 75 million jobs2.

How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

However, market failures have been common. Companies have underinvested in developing therapeutics for common diseases with poorly understood biological mechanisms, such as depression, anxiety and kidney disease, because they consider them too commercially risky or unprofitable to pursue3.

To address this gap, we propose an adapted innovation model based on mission-driven public–private partnerships (PPPs), in which government acts as a leading strategic investor. By bringing together the best scientists in academia and industry and lowering risks in industry development in areas of public need and for diseases with limited understanding, this model would accelerate translation, advance health and increase economic returns.

Here, we outline how it would work. It will require systems to ensure affordable access to drugs and therapies, as well as revenue sharing between public and private partners to guarantee public benefits and to support investments in innovation.

Complex diseases that affect swathes of the population create persistent health and economic burdens. Yet, the current biomedical innovation model has proved limited in addressing evolving health needs. Because private investment is guided by assessments of risk and return, it tends to favour diseases with well-defined biological mechanisms and high commercial potential. Diseases that are biologically complex, varied or associated with uncertain markets remain underexplored.

For example, in 2023, more than 300 million people globally had depression. The condition will cost the global economy an estimated $12 trillion between 2025 and 20504. In the United States in 2024, one in five people reported that they had received a diagnosis of major depressive disorder during their lifetime, resulting in an economic burden of $334 billion annually across health-care, household-related and workforce costs5. Yet, the leading drug class for depression (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) has remained unchanged since the 1970s6.

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

Other chronic diseases impose similarly large burdens. For example, chronic kidney disease affects around 800 million people worldwide — nearly one in seven — and is projected to become the fifth leading cause of death globally by 2040 if current trends continue7,8. Yet, existing therapies cannot stem its toll on human lives.

Antimicrobial resistance is another example, which is associated with 4.7 million deaths globally each year and could contribute to 10 million deaths annually by 2050. Increased treatment costs for people with resistant infections amount to $1 trillion every year9. The antibiotic development pipeline has been depleted over time as economic factors render companies’ return on investment lower than that for other drug classes9. These factors include insufficient funding for research and challenging business models, given the short duration of antibiotic treatments and the need to reserve successful new antibiotics as drugs of last resort, to be used after all other options have failed.

Bringing a therapy to market from discovery can take 10–15 years and cost anywhere between $880 million and $2.3 billion10,11. The majority (90%) of drug candidates fail after entering clinical studies, clinical trials and drug-approval processes12. And companies won’t invest if they are unsure whether a drug will be profitable.

Consequently, many diseases and conditions have no or few available therapies or only modestly effective options13. What’s needed is a mission-driven strategy to guide scientific capabilities and industry development towards areas of public need by elucidating biological mechanisms and aligning incentives for diseases in which market forces alone are insufficient14.

We propose addressing this misalignment of incentives by reconceptualizing the government’s role in therapeutic advancement through a model of mission-driven PPP. Complementing existing grant-based systems, the model would position the government as a principal investor in select areas of therapeutic development.

The government would thus influence which areas of health and science receive concentrated attention and how successful outcomes are deployed for the public good. Such a model could address specific national needs and global challenges. Here are seven components.

Technicians at work in a pharmaceutical factory.Credit: Getty

Select disease targets. We propose the establishment of a government-appointed independent advisory body or commission tasked with identifying priority disease targets using transparent, evidence-based criteria, including disease burden, economic cost, scientific readiness and demonstrable market failure. Further criteria to gauge and consider public input into the selection process could be implemented to ensure public trust.

Set up collaborations. A national government, acting alone or as part of an international consortium, would assume a leading role in supporting basic research into biological mechanisms. It would do so by bringing together basic scientists from academia and translational experts from industry to reduce risks in translational development. Private industry would contribute expertise in drug development, clinical trials, regulatory strategy, manufacturing and commercialization.

Provide initial investments. The proposed PPP would not replace existing grant-based systems or market-driven innovation; rather, it would act as a complement by targeting disease areas in which market risks and incentives consistently fail to generate sufficient private investment. The approach could yield fresh therapies and reduce the cost of care to society while generating revenue from new products.

Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?

Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?

In the United States, we propose a federal investment of one billion dollars annually over ten years, directed to specific disease areas. That is less than 1.8% of total US government spending on biomedical research, which was $54.5 billion in 2024. This would be supplemented by smaller investments of 10–20% of one billion dollars from a consortium of philanthropic foundations and industry partners joining the initiative in response to a request for application. Given the high costs of bringing a new drug to market, a $10-billion total investment should provide the scale and time needed to pursue about three major disease targets10–12.

Feed revenues back in. Public return is a defining feature of the PPP. Existing biomedical funding structures are mainly grant making, with the implication that public benefit will emerge indirectly through the downstream health improvements and economic growth spurred by discovery. By contrast, this PPP framework would directly incorporate public accountability as well as returns.

The government would need to leverage its status as a majority investor to ensure access, fair pricing and affordability. It might require conditions such as agreements to ensure access. Pricing frameworks could incorporate a value-based approach to pricing, in which health insurers offer reimbursements determined by a drug’s value for patients. Affordability conditions, such as reasonable-pricing clauses, would also serve as powerful leverage.

#1320. Raheem Sterling avoids jail for £270,000 Lamborghini crash: England star handed suspended prison sentence after telling court he underwent 12-day rehab stint for laughing gas 'problem'

Published: 04:50 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 14:13 EST, 25 November 2026

Former England football star Raheem Sterling avoided prison for dangerous driving and possession of nitrous oxide after it was revealed he spent 12 days in rehab.

The 31-year-old was handed a 12-month sentence, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court today and has been banned from driving for two years.

He was also ordered to complete 100 hours of community service and must pay a victim surcharge of £187 as well as prosecution costs of £85.

Sterling – who is currently without a club but has played for Liverpool, Manchester City and Chelsea – pleaded guilty after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini Urus SUV on May 28 while under the influence of laughing gas.

Four police forces received reports about the footballer's dangerous driving before he eventually crashed his car into a metal gate on the A327 in Hampshire during rush hour on the morning of May 28.

Sterling told police he had 'a problem' with laughing gas after subjecting rush hour motorists to a terrifying 90 minutes of dangerous driving, in which he zig-zagged on the M3 and M25 motorways before swerving onto a slip road and crashing into a metal gate. Police found six canisters of nitrous oxide in his car.

Raheem Sterling is pictured leaving Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Wednesday, shaking hands with his solicitor Leo Martin - he avoided prison time

Sterling is seen after being pulled over by police earlier this year while under the influence of laughing gas in his Lamborghini - he later spent 12 days in rehab

In the police station, Sterling was asked to judge 30 seconds with his eyes closed but was so impaired that he recorded 52.

The footballer – who wore trainers, a black quarter-zip jumper with a white t-shirt and black trousers – froze as he waited for the judge to enter the court room.

He sat with his back against the wall in the glass dock and kept eye contact with her while she read her sentencing remarks.

District Judge Kirsty Allman revealed that Sterling sought addiction treatment on June 15 and went into rehab for 12 days.

She explained that nitrous oxide had 'become a maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period in his career', adding that he was a 'role model'.

While his sentence does not mandate therapeutic intervention, the lead therapist at Banbury Lodge – where Sterling checked in – feels further treatment would be 'beneficial'.

His MBE, charitable work and time spent in rehabilitation were cited as mitigating factors, helping him avoid a prison sentence.

Allman added: 'You are 31 years old and a man of previous good character. I accept your character has been positively exemplary.

Sterling leaves the court with his solicitor having been given a suspended sentence

Image issued by the Crown Prosecution Service shows the damage to the Lamborghini Urus being driven by Sterling

'(But) these offences are so serious that neither a fine nor a community order can be justified. The custodial threshold is clearly crossed, and custody is unavoidable.'

However, custody was avoided because the law was changed in March 2026, with custodial sentences of one year or less presumed to be suspended – unless there are specific aggravating features – because of the overcrowded prison population.

Temporary chief inspector Chris Sharland of Hampshire Police said: 'Nitrous oxide, commonly known as laughing gas or NOS, is a Class C drug, and driving whilst under its influence is an emerging threat to the safety of motorists on our roads.

'Driving whilst impaired with nitrous oxide can cause unconsciousness, and in the worst-case scenarios neurological damage or death, so there is a very real risk of causing serious harm to yourself or other motorists.

'We urge drivers to be aware of not only the law, but the risk this type of behaviour carries – one decision can have devastating consequences.'

In his pre-sentencing remarks, Sterling's lawyer, Jason Bartfeld KC, said Sterling is 'more concerned not by damage to his reputation' but the 'consequences' it has had for his family, particularly his children.

He added: 'Mr Sterling recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position and has sought to address these in the most positive and effective way and with some success.

'All of it makes it extremely sad and a matter of his own personal regret, tarnishing his own personal reputation.

'The end point of this is that he is absolutely determined that he will never appear before a criminal court again.'

Police bodycam footage showed the moment that Sterling was arrested with canisters and a deflated balloon on his lap.

An officer could be heard saying 'you can put that down' to the footballer after opening his car door.

He could then be seen taking the items from his lap and putting them behind his seat.

Sterling gets back in the car after his sentencing and is banned from driving for two years

Sterling, who won the PFA Young Player of the Year award in 2018-19, was then read his rights while being arrested after being asked to put his arms behind his back.

There was a 40mph speed restriction on the M25 as he veered from lane to lane during peak travel time, with one witness fearing a ‘fatal collision’.

His arrest, near the Minley interchange, where the A327 meets the M3 in Hampshire, happened four weeks after he had returned to the UK following the end of an abortive attempt to revive his career at Dutch club Feyenoord.

Sterling, from Berkshire, pleaded guilty in September to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen after a single vehicle collision at 8.45am on May 28.

During that hearing, Basingstoke Magistrates' Court heard that Sterling was so impaired by the laughing gas that he was unable to perform basic police station tests like placing his finger on his nose or placing one foot in front of another.

Barrister Simon Jones, prosecuting, said of Sterling: 'He appeared to be quiet, withdrawn and lethargic and actively fidgeting.

'Eye lids drooping consistent with fatigue or drug impairment. He said he was feeling very cold, despite this being in the middle of a heatwave with 33-degree temperatures.'

The 31-year-old was charged with dangerous driving and possession of laughing gas after swerving his car on the M25 and M3

Motorist Fiona Jennings told police she had looked across to witness the driver of the Lamborghini with a balloon in front of his face which was so big she thought it was an air bag.

It was so big that 'she had no idea how the driver would have been able to see the road ahead,' Mr Jones said.

Ms Jennings described Sterling's driving as 'absolutely horrendous' and expressed 'genuine concern that the driver may kill someone'.

Evidence previously presented to court suggested Sterling was also inhaling laughing gas while at the wheel of the Lamborghini a full seven hours before his arrest.

A concerned witness called police after seeing the driver of the same car entering a McDonalds car park alarmingly fast at 1.10am the same morning and seeing the driver holding up 'a pink, inflated balloon'.

By 7.45am that morning, another motorist concerned by the Lamborghini erratically changing lanes saw the driver placing a white balloon to his mouth and inhaling its contents.

For 30 minutes, that motorist watched the vehicle weave between the inside and outside lanes and come close to smashing into the central reservation.

#1319. Be warned, JJ Gabriel: The SEVEN wonderkids who flopped after making high-profile moves - as Man United star, 16, closes in on move to Real Madrid - but there is cause for optimism

Published: 05:00 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 15:14 EST, 25 November 2026

In a sport obsessed with the next big thing, there is more attention than ever being paid to teenage prodigies who appear destined for the very top.

The latest player to have fans raving is former Manchester United academy star JJ Gabriel, 16, who joined the club aged nine but stunned those at Old Trafford by asking to leave. He is now closing in on a move to Real Madrid.

The acrimonious nature of the teenager's departure has left Gabriel vulnerable to a spectacular fall from grace, particularly after his team released montages showing him joining an agency and saying goodbye to United.

The spotlight is well and truly burning on Gabriel, and he would do well to learn the lessons of other youngsters who were tipped for greatness but ultimately crashed and burned.

Of course, injuries, personal issues and media pressure can all weigh heavily on a young player's prospects. There are countless pitfalls that mean tomorrow's stars often burn out before they have had the chance to shine.

Here, Daily Mail Sport runs the rule over some of the most famous wonderkids who never managed to live up to their potential.

Wonderkid JJ Gabriel, 16, confirmed his exit from Manchester United on Tuesday night

In 2004, Freddy Adu was viewed as the future of American football. Dubbed 'The Next Pele', the Ghanaian-born talent was the youngest professional athlete in major American sports when he signed his first contract at just 14.

The hype was extraordinary. He became MLS's highest-paid player, secured a lucrative Nike contract and appeared in an advert alongside Pele himself.

But things never quite worked out for the attacking midfielder. After three years at DC United and Real Salt Lake, he made the much-anticipated move to Europe, joining Benfica for £1million in 2007. It was largely downhill from there.

After making just 11 appearances in three years in Portugal, he moved to Monaco before embarking on a series of unsuccessful and increasingly disappointing loan spells in Portugal, Turkey and Greece. He eventually ended up at Brazilian club Bahia in 2013.

From that point, Adu floated around clubs in Brazil, Serbia, Finland, the US and Sweden. He last played competitive fooball for Swedish third-tier side Osterlen in 2021, aged 32. He remains one of football's biggest 'what if' stories.

Freddy Adu was dubbed 'The Next Pele' but he never fulfilled anywhere near his potential

Once described by Sir Alex Ferguson as 'the best player I have ever seen at his age', Ravel Morrison is a particularly unfortunate case of an English prospect failing to make the most of an extraordinarily promising career.

As a fresh-faced 17-year-old, he arrived at Carrington with the talent and ability to become one of the world's best players.

He had all the attributes of a world-class attacking midfielder and appeared mature beyond his years on the pitch. Off it, however, was a different story.

In early 2011, barely a year after signing his first professional contract with Manchester United, he was charged with witness intimidation in connection with a domestic violence case.

Since then, although he has never served time in prison, Morrison has faced several further charges, including assault, harassment and fraud. His repeated off-field troubles ultimately derailed a career that had once promised so much.

Morrison has gone on to represent 15 clubs during a career spanning 16 years, failing to fulfil the promise that once enchanted Ferguson. He is currently plying his trade in the second tier of UAE football.

Ravel Morrison was one of the most talented players to come through Man United's academy

The first Brazilian on this list is former Manchester City forward Robinho. Having come through the Santos academy – a production line that has also delivered the likes of Pele and Neymar – he was expected to become the next superstar to emerge from the club's illustrious ranks.

However, a series of setbacks meant he never quite fulfilled that early promise. Robinho followed in the footsteps of Brazilian stars such as Adriano, Dani Alves and Kaka by moving to Europe at a young age, joining Real Madrid in 2005.

He enjoyed a promising start to his career, making more than 100 appearances for Los Blancos and winning two league titles before turning 24.

But his move to Manchester City in 2008 failed to take his career to the next level. In fact, things began to unravel.

The Brazilian did not get off to the best of starts. Upon arriving in Manchester, he revealed that 'Chelsea had made a great proposal, and I accepted'.

What followed were two underwhelming years at the Etihad, where he scored 16 goals in 53 appearances and spent much of his second season in England sidelined by injury.

Robinho subsequently joined AC Milan before spells with a number of Turkish clubs and a return to Brazil. He never again reached the heights of his early career.

The Brazilian is currently imprisoned after being found guilty of sexual assault in connection with an incident at a Milan nightclub in 2013. He began serving his nine-year sentence in 2024.

Former Man City star Robinho never quite fulfilled the early promise he had back in Brazil

Another case reminiscent of Adu's: a young superstar who was seemingly rated too highly before we ever really got to see him play.

Mastour caught the eye of Italian giants AC Milan after gaining notoriety on YouTube. His video, uploaded in 2012 and titled 'The Best 14-year-old in the World', showcased the Moroccan's impressive array of skills and tricks, making him one of football's first viral sensations.

The hype surrounding Mastour was staggering, with the youngster securing a lucrative endorsement deal with Nike. Before long, he was posing alongside Neymar in a photoshoot.

But the success never materialised for the tricky forward. During four years on AC Milan's books, he failed to make a single first-team appearance and managed just six outings during loan spells at Malaga and Dutch side PEC Zwolle.

The Moroccan, now 28, plays in the fourth tier of Italian football. Quite how such a highly rated prospect failed to fulfil his potential remains a mystery.

Hachim Mastour dazzled as a teenager on the internet but ended up a long way from the top

From one player who never showed his quality to one who only a decade ago was the recipient of the coveted Golden Boy award for the best under-21 player in Europe.

Renato Sanches was an absolute phenomenon, the box-to-box midfielder burst onto the scene in the 2015-16 season at Benfica – earning himself a place on the plane to France with Portugal for the 2016 Euros where he played a pivotal role in his nation's triumph.

Those performances saw a host of European giants fight it out to land the then-18-year-old, with Bayern Munich emerging triumphant – landing the midfielder in a deal rising to £63million.

However, Sanches failed to hit his stride in Germany and he was soon shipped out on loan to Swansea – where he was best remembered for passing the ball to an advertising hoarding.

He enjoyed a small resurgence at Lille, winning Ligue 1 and the French Super Cup, paving the way for a move to PSG. But once again, the big transfer failed to work out, and he now finds himself with Greek side Panathinaikos.

He enjoyed a resurgence at Lille, winning Ligue 1 and the French Super Cup, which paved the way for a move to Paris Saint-Germain.

But once again, a big-money move failed to work out, and he now finds himself at Greek side Panathinaikos.

Renato Sanches (pictured at Roma in 2024) now plies his trade in Greece with Panathinaikos

Alexandre Pato had the world at his feet, but his body ultimately failed to deliver on the extraordinary talent he possessed.

The Brazilian was an electric centre-forward who lit up European football. His goal against Barcelona in the Champions League, scored after just 24 seconds at the age of 22, was a perfect illustration of his frightening ability.

His pace, agility and clinical finishing saw him touted as a future world-beater, while he was named Golden Boy.

Alexandre Pato is another wonderkid who saw their career hampered by a string of injuries

Yet persistent injury problems made it almost impossible for Pato to fulfil his early promise.

The Brazilian struggled with ankle, Achilles and muscle problems throughout his career. As the injuries mounted, his outstanding physical attributes began to wane, rendering the qualities that had once terrified defenders increasingly ineffective.

After six years at AC Milan, Pato returned to Brazil to join Corinthians. He spent two years with the club before embarking on short spells at Chelsea and Villarreal, neither of which yielded lasting success.

Rounding off this list is another English talent who once looked destined for the very top but has since seen his career take a downward turn.

Back in 2019, there were few hotter prospects in world football than Jadon Sancho. The then 19-year-old had made the brave decision two years earlier to leave England, having spent several impressive years in Manchester City's academy, and join Bundesliga giants Borussia Dortmund.

It seemed a bizarre move at the time, but the switch proved to be a stroke of genius. Sancho was handed regular first-team football and flourished, registering 40 goals and 54 assists in just 118 Bundesliga appearances. He also collected a DFB-Pokal winner's medal.

By 2021, the boy from Kennington had the world at his feet, with a host of suitors willing to break the bank to secure his services.

Jadon Sancho once had the world at his feet but has found himself stuck in a downward spiral

After a summer-long transfer saga, Sancho eventually joined Manchester United for an eye-watering £73million, reportedly earning £350,000 per week. It proved to be a nightmare move for both parties.

The Englishman had to wait until late November to score his first United goal in his debut season and never consistently rediscovered his best form.

In January 2024, he returned to Germany and enjoyed a revival, helping guide Dortmund to the Champions League final, where they lost to Real Madrid at Wembley.

Two unsuccessful loan spells at Chelsea and Aston Villa followed before Sancho left United as a free agent last summer. He remains without a club at the age of 26, just five years after his mega-money move.

For all the promising youngsters who struggle to live up to the hype, there are also teen sensations who navigate the pitfalls of professional football to achieve great things.

Kylian Mbappe helped Monaco win their first Ligue 1 title for 17 years having broken into the team as a 16-year-old. His progress since then has been remarkable and he remains one of the world's very best at Real Madrid.

His team-mate Vinicius Jr signed for Real Madrid to much fanfare as an 18-year-old and has lived up to it all for both club and country.

While you could argue that Neymar could have achieved more, he has still enjoyed a stellar career across the globe and become the highest-scoring Brazilian player in history for the national side after signing for Barcelona, as one of the most talked-about starlets.

Wayne Rooney broke through for Everton at 16 and went on to have a brilliant career

When you look closer to home, Wayne Rooney and Michael Owen broke through as exciting 16-year-olds and both reached the very highest level.

Paolo Maldini made his AC Milan debut at 16 and became one of the all-time great centre-backs and Cesc Fabregas developed into a world class midfielder after getting selected at the same age for Arsenal.

Going back further, Diego Maradona was playing senior football at 15, as did Ronaldo Nazario, while Lionel Messi embarked on his extraordinary career at 16.

JJ Gabriel and his management will be hoping that when all is said and done - his name is associated with this category and avoid joining the starlets who never quite made it.

#1318. How acidic compounds in human sweat open a mosquito ion channel

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Swathi Pantheerayil is in the CSIR–Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad 500007, India, and in the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research, Ghaziabad, India.

Janesh Kumar is in the CSIR–Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad 500007, India, and in the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research, Ghaziabad, India.

Female mosquitoes use several sensory systems to locate a host whose blood they can feed on. One of these systems is a group of proteins known as ionotropic receptors, which detect the acidic compounds in human sweat that contribute to its sour smell. Writing in Nature, Xu et al.1 report 3D structures of an ionotropic-receptor complex from the malaria-spreading mosquito Anopheles stephensi. The structures show how the binding of an acid activates the receptor, which then opens its ion-conducting pore and generates an electrical signal that helps to guide the mosquito towards a human host.
