Sunderland fans are urging their side to press at every opportunity, cheering each time an intervention is successful. Still, we wait for the first notable chance.

Mukiele is down after being caught in the face by Calvert-Lewin as they both challenged for a high ball. There was no malice in the striker’s attempt to win possession and play swiftly continues following some quick treatment for Mukiele.

Mukiele was gearing up for a long throw, but the Sunderland defender held onto the ball for too long, with referee Attwell sounding his whistle to give possession back to Leeds.

Ampadu’s long throw-in casuses some momentary chaos in Sunderland’s six-yard box. However, the linesman’s flag is raised and Leeds’ chance disappears.

It’s been a scrappy opening to this game. Mukiele tries a very ambitious effort from long range, but he drags the shot well wide and it harmlessly trickles out of play.

O’Nein defends unconvincingly as he battles with Calvert-Lewin and attempts to deal with a long ball. The centre back just about handles the situation and prevents the striker from carving out a one-on-one opportunity.

On his return to the Sunderland line-up, Brobbey tests Trafford in Sunderland’s first attack. The striker’s deflected effort bounces awkwardly in front of the goalkeeper, who parries the ball out for a corner. Leeds then defend the set-piece well and clear the danger.

That was a deceptively hard save for James Trafford to make to deny Brian Brobbey. Although the connection was not the cleanest, that almost made it harder as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. Leeds are dominating the ball in these early exchanges. Sunderland look slightly unsettled so far. Bogle is pushing particularly far forward for the visitors.

Wilson starts for Leeds. The Welshman was pivotal for Fulham last season. His Leeds career is yet to meaningfully get going, but he has a great chance to impress today.

Leeds get us under way here. How will come out on top in these feisty northern weather conditions?

My favourite part of every Sunderland game is the singing of Elvis Presley’ Can’t Help Falling in Love before kick off. Not sure the “The King” had a football club on Wearside in mind when he wrote it but it just works as a pre-match anthem. I also grew up in a house where there was a lot of Elivs playing when I was a small child. Anyway, on to the football.

The Stadium of Light is in fantastic spirits as per usual, despite Sunderland floundering in 20th position. Can the home side record a much-needed win to ignite their domestic season?

Starting good in the season, we are really keen to follow our goals for our system where we train every week and we follow how our team should play.

And, how the XI plus the subs should play together, fight for each other, and we have to keep on going like this. We know how good Sunderland are.

The team is good. Obviously, every team has a different start in the season but still we know what this team can do. Last year they achieved Europe so it is a really big thing.

We know the players and, yeah, we know how hard these games can be but we are here to try to win and to take all the points.

It is going to be a tough one. Also, the weather, I think. The wind is unbelievable but we are ready. We are here and ready to fight.

We go into every game confident and ready to fight for the three points. We are here to win. We are going for every game [because] we want to win so we will try our best and fight.

Right now, I think his intensity against the ball, his workload against the ball, is on a way better level in comparison to how it was when he arrived and as soon as he adapts, I’m pretty sure his quality will shine through sooner rather than later.

Leeds are always a good side, it was in the Championship and now in the Premier League.

They are doing really well, they are consistent as well. They built momentum early in the season, which is always good, so they are in a different position but anything is possible in football. We think that it is going to be a new opportunity to get better.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Sunderland: Roefs, Hume, Mukiele, O’Nien, Reinildo, Xhaka, Sadiki, Le Fée, Rigg, Angulo, BrobbeySubs: Ellborg, Methalie, Alderete, Diarra, Ahoka, Talbi, Fofana, Angulo, Tuterov

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

#1298. Sporting Lisbon vs Manchester United RECAP: Visitors held in controversial and chaotic thriller as Liverpool beat Club Brugge

By HARRY BAMFORTH, LIVE SPORTS COVERAGE REPORTER and LUKE POWER, SPORTS REPORTER

Relive Daily Mail Sport's coverage from Wednesday's Champions League action as Manchester United travelled to Sporting Lisbon while Liverpool took on Club Brugge.

It's not every day that you get to spend an evening with Harry Bamforth and Luke Power - and we wouldn't recommend it, either.

Thanks for putting up with us, especially when the football is hard enough to cope with as it is if you're a Manchester United fan.

Do joins us in the morning as the reaction and fall-out from the Champions League action continues interminably.

Here are the Premier League fixtures at the weekend:

Senne Lammens' two errors cost Man United victory at Sporting

CHRIS WHEELER AT JOSE ALVALADE STADIUM: A week into the job and Mauricio Pochettino must be getting used to the madness of Manchester United.

Liverpool showed a bit of everything tonight: possession dominance in the first half, counter-attacking prowess in the second, and defensive solidity throughout (for the most part!).

Lewis Steele was on hand to bring you his thoughts from Belgium.

Club Brugge 0-3 Liverpool: Reds close in on qualification

LEWIS STEELE AT JAN BREYDEL STADION: A brace for Isak and another from Wirtz fired the Reds to victory in Bruges after their strikes helped Liverpool get back to winning ways in Europe.

Normally I post all the goals and crazy moments separately, but there were just too many tonight.

So, instead, you can catch all the chaos in the highlights on YouTube. From penalties and howlers to disallowed goals and sending-offs, this game had it all.

Rio Ngumoha is averaging 7.8 completed dribbles every match in this year's Champions League.

No player with at least 300 minutes played has done better since 2006-07. Full credit to Opta for this one. One man has done more this campaign, and that's Jeremy Doku on 11.9, but he doesn't have the 300 minutes under his belt.

Let it sink in. When we think of direct, unstoppable dribblers, we think of Lionel Messi, Neymar, Khvichia Kvaratskhelia. Oddly Thomas Partey was up there in the standings one season. But those world-class wingers, Ngumoha is up there with them for pure dribbling ability at the moment. It's a long career ahead, and you hope his spark won't be muted, but he has mad a dazzling start. If he can add goals and assists, his potential is sky-high.

Manchester United may have been done over by some decisions, I know, but not all of them were wrong.

The penalty conceded by Senne Lammens? Stonewall.

So that means the next stat I am about to share is a pretty damning indictment of United's season (bar the Leny Yoro red, before you all have a pop at me).

Man United have received five red cards and conceded five penalties in just 17 games across all competitions this season.

Liverpool couldn't have had a better week going into the Merseyside derby than beating Manchester United and Brugge 7-0 on aggregate.

The annoying thing for Andoni Iraola is that Victor Munoz has picked up a knock, and he had to bring on Rio Ngumoha earlier than expected as a result, so that inhibits his options and energy up front ever so slightly.

But he will be greatly encouraged by how his £100m+ men, namely Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, and Bradley Barcola, are melding. We're yet to see the best from the latter on a consistent basis. That's the final piece of the puzzle.

Wirtz is flying now - he has now scored or assisted or done both in seven of his last nine games in the Premier League and Champions League.

Everton are having a good season and will be right up for it, but Liverpool have teed themselves up for a good performance at midday on Sunday.

Mauricio Pochettino, Man United boss, speaking to TNT Sports:

Here's the Alisson assist from earlier. Playmaker stuff from Liverpool's number one. Always thought he could have played outfield.

Manchester United just hate playing away in Europe.

United are now winless in their last seven Champions League away games (D3 L4).

Their worst-ever run is eight... which they could well match after playing their final away match in the league phase in January.

#1297. Mauricio Pochettino is creating a siege mentality straight out of Sir Alex Ferguson's playbook - the refereeing horror show in Lisbon is just more ammunition, writes NATHAN SALT

Published: 02:10 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 02:50 EST, 26 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino's job at Manchester United is hard enough without match officials getting in his way.

He's got to raise the physical floor of this team, embed a high-press playing style that's at odds with the laxer approach of predecessor Michael Carrick, rid this group of individual mistakes that continue to plague the dressing room, battle against mounting injuries and suspensions, work with a modest transfer budget, navigate the press, create an identity that appears to have been lost and do it all playing every three to four days.

But where Carrick looked eager to put out fires – part of his original appeal to bosses was his ability to steer clear of the headlines his predecessor, Ruben Amorim, brought with such frequency - Pochettino is keen to pour petrol on them and it's lit a fire that everyone inside the building is embracing. It's straight out of Sir Alex Ferguson's playbook.

Pochettino grew up idolising the greatness of Ferguson and when they shared a private lunch together in 2016, it would become a key moment in Pochettino's own managerial journey to here, now the man leading Manchester United.

In Ferguson's mind, and this was shared with Pochettino that day over lunch, he must spin two plates simultaneously to thrive at a club the size of United.

The very best coaches can play a game on the pitch and one in the press. To Ferguson, winning off the pitch was as crucial as winning on it.

Mauricio Pochettino has shown in the space of a week how he can channel Sir Alex Ferguson

A lot of what Pochettino has done thus far feels like it's straight out of idol Ferguson's playbook

'Sir Alex Ferguson represents everything that I admire from a coach, a head coach, a man, a manager and I think he represents my values. I really admire him,' Pochettino recently said. It shows.

So much of what Pochettino has done so far has got Ferguson's fingerprints all over it. They were all over the pre-match interview ahead of the Sporting clash when he was asked about his start to life in Manchester.

'You've had a game as Manchester United manager now…' the interviewer began.

To which Pochettino replied: 'No. I've had EIGHT minutes,' referencing the small section against Liverpool prior to Leny Yoro's unjust sending off.

Those same fingerprints were also over the club's fiercely front-footed response to ProRef following the decision for Yoro's red to be overturned. Howard Webb doubled down on the original decision, a call Pochettino and the club believed was 'totally wrong'. United are now taking up their irritation with the Premier League. Top flight referees are understood to be livid.

And then there's Lisbon, a night of total chaos, most inflicted by referee Szymon Marciniak who chalked off a legitimate goal for Amad due to a non-foul by Youri Tielemans, which he was booked for. Marciniak would later send Tielemans off having already chalked off a match-winning goal for United due to an alleged infringement by Patrick Dorgu on the goalkeeper. All of this came after he was conned into giving a penalty against Lisandro Martinez. Pochettino bounced around his technical area like Tigger, apoplectic at the unjustness of it all.

He will wait on another apology that will do nothing other than play into the siege mentality he is trying to create.

Pochettino has only been in the building a week and already he is embracing the spirit of Ferguson. Where that would lead Ferguson's United to major finals and titles, now it could be the key to Pochettino salvaging a season that has threatened to get majorly out of hand.

Pochettino's fury at decisions made against his team are protecting this fragile dressing room

Pochettino has proven to have a firm grip on the media side so far, dictating the narratives

His first training session, which exposed his desire to play Bryan Mbeumo out wide, use a back-three at times in possession, and have Joshua Zirkzee as a focal point, was recorded on a rogue drone that soon published its findings on YouTube. More than 100,000 views later it disappeared.

Then the trip to Anfield where Yoro was shown a straight red card – wrongly – for a last-man foul on Alexander Isak. An independent panel retrospectively overturned the decision 5-0, even if ProRef chief Howard Webb doubled down to back the original call.

Pochettino, armed with research, even pointed out how the opening goal from Dominik Szoboszlai should not have stood due to illegal interference with the defensive wall by Liverpool's Bradley Barcola.

Many had not even got that on the rap sheet. Pochettino cleverly planted another seed of injustice.

'Maybe the rules changed while I was in America?' Pochettino said sarcastically.

'Why didn't they check it? It should have been disallowed. I'm here to defend my players and my club.'

And so a furious United headed for Lisbon and were subjected to abysmal officiating that played into Pochettino's hands in terms of masking the individual errors that were as costly as the officials.

Bruno Fernandes scored a brace in Portugal on a night where Pochettino's ideas were obvious

His demonstrative nature on touchline contrasts to Michael Carrick - and players responded

'It's difficult to find a game where you get punished in one game,' Pochettino said. 'We were punished a lot in key actions.'

Ferguson would defend players publicly and point fingers at officials and Pochettino has so far proven to be no different.

On a night where goalkeeper Senne Lammens made two particularly costly errors, a sign of his struggles this season, Pochettino embraced him on the pitch and in the media. If anything, the defence in front of the Belgian had to shoulder the manager's blame.

Noussair Mazraoui, too, was culpable of really poor positioning for Sporting's opening goal, just like Matthijs de Ligt was at Anfield. In back-to-back matches, Pochettino has finished with 10 men. Each and every player got nothing but universal backing publicly.

Players are looking to the touchline and seeing a head coach they can respond to. Players unquestionably let down Carrick and have done their level best to drag Pochettino down in moments, too, but he's demonstrative, emotional and a totemic figure for them to rally behind.

There were signs in Lisbon of the identity that Pochettino is imprinting, signs of the high-press style, signs of a structure that has been so badly lacking, signs of a plan, a method to lifting them off the canvas and have them back swinging punches domestically and in Europe. There were signs, too, that Pochettino and his staff have lots of work to do to flush this dressing room of the mistake culture that has crept in.

By pointing fingers at the officials, Pochettino is shielding this fragile dressing room from even more scrutiny than it has already faced. Just like his managerial idol, he's proving a master of creating the siege mentality that could be the key to getting United out of the mess he's inherited them in.

'He persuaded us Manchester United are the team everyone loves to hate,' Ryan Giggs famously said of Ferguson in 2022.

'He makes us feel everyone wants us to come second and it is us against the world. He lays down the challenge for you to take up.'

Now it's Pochettino who is creating his own version. Watching his protege from the stands, no doubt Ferguson is beaming with pride.

#1295. Aussie mum's well-meaning act to get kids off their screens sparks council crackdown and $800 fines - after 'joyless' neighbours complained about her soccer pitch on public land

Published: 03:16 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 03:16 EST, 26 November 2026

An Aussie mum who set up donated soccer goals on a vacant block of council land to create a thriving neighbourhood pitch says she has been threatened with huge fines.

After complaints from neighbours, described by one local as 'joyless', Brisbane City Council dispatched its Rapid Response ranger team to the site.

The mum behind the initiative, Graceville resident Madeline Ruffino, told Daily Mail she had been ordered by the council to remove the goals after every game or face an $834 fine for each one left behind.

She is now leading a neighbourhood revolt against the council, with more than 1,000 people signing a petition calling for the donated goals to be allowed to stay.

What began with a handful of children kicking a ball around on an empty block on Long Street East quickly grew into a popular after-school and weekend gathering spot after Ms Ruffino installed the soccer goals.

Residents maintained the grass, marked out two pitches and secured donated equipment from Brisbane Paralympic Football Program director Jay Larkins.

Parents were thrilled to see their children spending hours outside with friends rather than glued to their screens.

For many children living in townhouses with little or no outdoor space, the vacant block became their shared backyard.

Residents marked out football pitches on this inner-Brisbane block and helped maintain the grass

Madeline Ruffino is fighting to keep donated soccer goals available for children on council-owned land

Councillor Nicole Johnston said council policy prevents the soccer goals from being left on the land

Ms Ruffino said the council's order to remove the goals after every game was impractical.

'We live in a townhouse complex. We don't have sheds or large backyards, and we simply have nowhere to store multiple goals, particularly the larger ones that were so generously donated to these kids.

'They weren't hurting anyone. They were just playing.'

But after being threatened with fines, Ruffino reluctantly packed away the larger goals and made smaller ones available from her front yard for children to borrow and return.

Since then, she said the number of children coming out to play had dwindled, with some arriving with their football boots and balls but quickly leaving when they discovered the goals were gone.

Ms Ruffino said that older children in the neighbourhood already had limited options when it came to playing outdoors.

'We've got security guards walking school grounds on weekends to stop kids playing there,' she said.

'Parks are fantastic for younger children, but older kids need somewhere to go too. Somewhere they can kick a ball, meet their friends, meet new friends and feel welcome.

Many nearby families live in townhouses with little or no backyard, making the space a popular meeting place

Council’s Rapid Response team visited the community football space following complaints before referring the matter to its Parks team

Organisers say they want a practical compromise and are not seeking exclusive use of the public land

Brisbane Paralympic Football Program director Jay Larkins donated goals and offered 10 new footballs

'We encourage kids to get off their screens and spend time outside, but we need to give them places where they're actually allowed to do that.'

The vacant land was acquired by the council through property buybacks following the Brisbane floods of 2011 and 2022.

Tennyson Ward councillor Nicole Johnston told Daily Mail that children were permitted to play soccer on the vacant land, but council policy prohibited sporting equipment from being stored there.

'Children can play soccer on the open space in Long St East, Graceville. I have communicated this message clearly to residents for many months,' she said.

'However, council policy does not allow sporting facilities to be stored on parkland or open space, and sports fields and facilities do not adjoin residential properties due to adverse amenity impacts and property damage to neighbours.'

Cr Johnston said formal sporting fields were generally maintained to a higher safety standard for organised sport.

She suggested residents store the goals on private property, bring them onto the land when children wanted to play, and remove them afterwards.

She also pointed to several alternative recreational spaces, including Bert St Clair Oval, about 500 metres away, a park in neighbouring Sherwood and Gordon Thompson Oval in Chelmer.

But Ms Ruffino has vowed not to give up on the neighbourhood children.

'They may be making us remove the goals, but I'm not going to stop helping these kids play.'

#1294. Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick

Hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

More than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

An announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

At 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a new manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the new head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

What a finish from Rayan to give Bournemouth the lead! 🔥 https://t.co/9BV0G5Tqgi

The outstanding Rayan should have had a hat-trick but failed to take two chances in the second half, when he only had goalkeeper Senne Lammens to beat, after Bournemouth had already doubled their lead. It came as Leny Yoro slipped over and presented the ball straight to Adrien Truffert, who squared it for Marcus Tavernier to side-foot home. It was that ridiculously easy.

The third was the same, with Evanilson chasing down a ball forward by Tyler Adams. The striker should not have got there. But Harry Maguire, captain in Fernandes’s absence, gave up, pointing at Lammens to win it. Instead, the goalkeeper was beaten to the ball and Evanilson’s finish from an angle, arcing high into the net, was superb.

"What a finish!" 😮‍💨 Evanilson makes it 3-0 to Bournemouth with a stunning goal https://t.co/hPMR78Z3cX

“You’re going down with the City,” goaded the Bournemouth fans and it is that end of the table United need to fret about. Which means, for Carrick, it has to be over. The Stretford End sang his name. But it was out of support for him as a player, his reputation, what he represented, not what is happening now as they once again vented their anger at the owners, director of football, Jason Wilcox, and even the plans for a new stadium.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a new nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have big characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He says: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He says: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

“Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”

Carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

“A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

#1293. Frustrated Mauricio Pochettino accuses referee of 'punishing' Man United in chaotic Sporting Lisbon draw after having TWO goals ruled out - as former star Ashley Young labels official's performance as a 'disgrace'

Published: 18:55 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 03:19 EST, 26 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino was left frustrated after Manchester United were ‘punished’ by more controversial refereeing decisions in Lisbon on Wednesday night.

Three days after Pochettino was left raging over Leny Yoro’s early red card at Anfield, United were held to a 2-2 Champions League draw by Sporting after conceding two penalties and having two goals disallowed by Polish referee Szymon Marciniak who also sent off Youri Tielemans.

‘It’s difficult to find a game where you get punished so much in one game. We were punished a lot in key actions,’ said Pochettino.

Asked if the decision to rule out Amad Diallo’s goal before half-time and book Tielemans was particularly harsh, the United manager remained tight-lipped but nodded.

‘It’s difficult to answer because I think everyone knows it’s impossible to understand why that happened on the field,’ added Pochettino before adding sarcastically: ‘I think it's a good welcome for us after seven days! Today it's going to be my first week in charge.

‘Through our experience, if we go back and remember circumstances in different clubs, things like this you will suffer because it's the circumstance that always is against us.’

Mauricio Pochettino gave his verdict on the performance of referee Szymon Marciniak

Marciniak was at the centre of several controversial decisions as United drew 2-2 with Sporting

Pochettino also defended his goalkeeper Senne Lammens who was at fault for both Sporting’s goals despite saving a penalty.

‘Football is about making mistakes,’ he said. ‘I want to support always my player. It's something that happened in that case.

‘It's our responsibility too to provide the best tools. I think in this type of action also our defensive line needs to cover better the keeper because it was very difficult.

‘It's to blame us because I think we need to manage better this type of situation. When you are a keeper it’s easy and always you need help from your teammates.’

Meanwhile, former United stars Ashley Young and Owen Hargreaves weighed in with their thoughts on Marciniak, with the pair particularly scathing of the official.

Speaking on the BBC, Young said: ’The referee’s performance was just simply wow... the decisions that he gave.

’Youri Tielemans getting sent off because you booked him when it should never have been a booking, and it should have been an equalising goal.

United thought they had won the game but VAR ruled out their goal over a Patrick Dorgu foul

’The third goal should have stood because he’s saying Patrick Dorgu fouled the keeper. The keeper comes out and flaps at it before he is even touched. How that has gone to VAR is beyond me.

‘His decision making today is nothing more than a disgrace.’

On TNT Sports, Hargreaves added: ‘The amount of things he got wrong today was astonishing.

'People don’t come to the game to hear you blow your whistle.’

#1291. O'Brien's 'No Excuses' Verdict & Merseyside Derby Message

Jake O’Brien says there are “no excuses” for Everton’s 4-0 defeat to Brentford on Monday, but believes Sunday’s Merseyside derby could provide the perfect motivation to bounce back.

A below-par display saw the Blues – reduced to 10 men after James Tarkowski’s first-half red card – defeated at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking after the game, defender O’Brien said: “It was really bad from start to finish.

“It was a knock-on effect of decisions and mistakes, and it carried on from there, really.

#1290. Care Leavers Tour Hill Dickinson Stadium

Hill Dickinson Stadium welcomed some of Liverpool’s care experienced young people for an exclusive behind-the-scenes tour to mark National Care Leavers Month.

A group of 25 care leavers, who have either left or are preparing to leave local authority care, were given the opportunity to explore the Club’s stunning waterfront home.

Observed every November, National Care Leavers Month is a UK-wide campaign that celebrates care experienced young people, amplifies their voices and promotes positive change in policy and practice.

The youngsters, many of whom were visiting a football stadium for the first time, enjoyed an informative tour of the state-of-the-art venue, including the impressive home dressing room, the Media Centre, pitchside areas and learning about the heritage of the historic site.

Jenny Glennard, Corporate Director of Children & Young People’s Services at Liverpool City Council, said: "On behalf of Liverpool Children's Social Care, I would like to again extend my gratitude to Everton for providing our care experienced young people with the fantastic opportunity to visit Hill Dickinson Stadium as part of National Care Leavers Month.

"To be given a personal group tour was an experience and memory they will never forget. All of our young people have expressed how much they enjoyed the day and how impressed they were with the stadium, as well as the staff who made them feel so welcome.

"We value our relationship with Everton and look forward to continuing to work with the Club in the future."

Liverpool City Council's Leaving Care Services provide a wide range of support for young people transitioning from local authority care.

Using a person-centred approach to independent living skills, planning and assessment, the service aims to improve outcomes across education, training, employment, health and accommodation.

For more information on Liverpool City Council's Leaving Care Services, click here.

#1289. Everton Announces Partnership With Global Power Technology Brand NOCO

Everton has announced a new multi-year partnership with global power technology brand NOCO.

The agreement will see the US-headquartered company become Everton’s 'Official Battery Charging Partner', further strengthening the Club’s growing portfolio of international commercial partners.

Founded in Cleveland, Ohio in 1914, NOCO has established itself as an internationally-recognised name in power technology, specialising in battery chargers, portable jump starters, tyre inflators, lithium batteries and related accessories.

With more than 110 years of innovation behind it, the company has developed a significant international presence, with offices and operations spanning North America, Europe, Asia and Australia.

As part of the partnership, NOCO will benefit from prominent brand visibility across Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, with LED perimeter advertising and exposure through the Club’s digital and social media channels.

The agreement will also provide NOCO with opportunities to host international clients and business guests and events at Everton fixtures at Hill Dickinson Stadium, using the Club’s matchday experiences to develop relationships and support its global business network.

Mark Rollings, Chief Partnerships Officer at Everton, said: “We are delighted to welcome NOCO to Everton. 

“NOCO is a well-established and respected international business with a proud heritage, a strong reputation for innovation and clear ambitions for continued global growth.

“Securing a brand of NOCO’s standing in a new commercial category is another positive step in the development of our partnership portfolio. It also demonstrates Everton’s growing profile and the opportunities we can offer international businesses looking to build their brand through the global reach of the Premier League. 

“NOCO joins an impressive group of globally recognised businesses already working with Everton, and we look forward to building a successful relationship that supports its continued growth.”

The partnership comes at a time of continued international expansion for NOCO, which has strengthened its presence in key overseas markets, including a recent agreement with AUTOBACS Global, one of Japan’s leading automotive retailers.

NOCO was also recently recognised at the 2026 Circana Automotive Aftermarket Performance Awards, winning the Maintenance & Repair category for achieving the highest increase in US market share.

Zachary Koehler, Partnership Marketing Manager at NOCO, said: We’re proud to partner with Everton, a club with a rich history and one of the most passionate fanbases in world football.

“Like Everton, NOCO is built on more than a century of heritage and a drive to keep moving forward. As we continue to grow internationally, the global reach of the Premier League gives us a powerful platform to connect with new audiences, customers, and partners. 

“We can’t think of a better way to make our debut than the Merseyside derby, and we look forward to a successful partnership with everyone at Everton." 

The agreement will see NOCO branding formally make its debut at Everton’s next home fixture, the Merseyside derby, and further underlines the Club’s growing commercial momentum and international appeal. NOCO joins an expanding portfolio of globally recognised brands associated with Everton, including Pepsi, Budweiser, Castore, Red Bull, Heinz, Nestlé, JYSK and Christopher Ward.

#1288. Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner

“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”

Kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and said: “You held it together. You got through it.” It showed how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

Kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

Kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

Bayern Munich and England's Ballon d'Or winner doing what he does best 🎯 https://t.co/yWNburqkpg

For his club, that is 19 goals more than any other player in the top five European leagues. And the most since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014-15. Kane won last season’s Golden Shoe by nine goals from Erling Haaland. He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Neither Kylian Mbappé nor Lamine Yamal, his closest rivals, scored in any finals.

Both gave interviews declaring why they should win the Ballon d’Or. Kane? “I don’t like talking about myself,” he said. “The 73 goals speak for themselves.” They do.

Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. Take his two goals against the Democratic Republic of Congo at the World Cup that saved his team and Thomas Tuchel from an embarrassing early exit.

The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

“A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments,” Prince William wrote on Instagram.

Kane, the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the award, is also the ultimate team player – so fulfilling that “collective performance” criteria – and a captain who leads by example on and off the pitch. Fair play? He was last booked in January and was cautioned just three times in 68 games and not at all in any of his 13 appearances this season.

And he works hard, so very hard. Kane was in the top 10 for total distance covered at the World Cup, despite playing a game fewer than most of the others on the list. And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

That work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and said he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

They probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

For the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more important than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

Kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

There's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN

Hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

First up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany said: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”

The plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has announced Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before quickly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

#1287. Welcome to the Man United madhouse, Mauricio! Man United emerge from the chaos at Sporting Lisbon with a draw as Senne Lammens joins their band of self-saboteurs in game that had it all, writes CHRIS WHEELER

Published: 17:18 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 05:01 EST, 26 November 2026

A week into the job and Mauricio Pochettino must be getting used to the madness of Manchester United by now.

If it's not drones flying over the training ground, red card controversies and random divots of grass, it's his own players shooting themselves in the foot.

At least, Pochettino emerged from the craziness in Lisbon with a draw on a night when Bruno Fernandes celebrated his return to the Jose Alvalade Stadium with a couple of goals.

But these are the kind of nights that must drive coaches like Pochettino potty. After the carnage of Michael Carrick's final two games in charge against Roma and Aston Villa, and the rancour of the Argentine's introduction to the Old Trafford circus at Anfield on Sunday, this was another mad, mad spectacle.

Where do we start? The two acts of self-sabotage by goalkeeper Senne Lammens? United's two disallowed goals? The first was harsh on the scorer, Amad Diallo, but also Youri Tielemans who received a booking that led to his sending-off in injury-time. Or maybe that divot, which Fernandes claimed he created and then hit to put United ahead with a bizarre deflected goal?

At the end of all the chaos, United had conceded five penalties in their last five games and picked up four red cards.

Senne Lammens (left) two errors cost Man United a deserving win at Sporting as they drew

New United head coach Mauricio Pochettino comforts Lammens at full-time after his mistakes

That is not something that will sit well with Pochettino. But after venting his frustration with the officiating over Leny Yoro's sending-off at Anfield, which dominated the build-up to this game after it was rescinded, here was another sequence of events that seemed to conspire against him.

It's not as if the Jose Alvalade Stadium was a cauldron of emotion to scramble the senses of the two sets of players and match officials either. Fernandes got a polite round of applause from the fans and a framed memento from his old club before kick-off.

When the teams came out, he was one of three former United players alongside Cristiano Ronaldo and Luis Nani honoured on a tifo of the Sporting Lisbon greats.

It was all very flat until the half-hour mark when United self-imploded again. Geny Catamo picked up the ball on the edge of the United box and teased Lisandro Martinez, playing at left back.

Martinez took the bait and stuck his leg out. He barely caught Sporting's No 10 and it took Catamo a full second to realise he had, before going down theatrically and earning a very soft penalty from Polish referee Szymon Marciniak.

Sporting's top scorer Luis Suarez stepped up and made it easy for Lammens to make the save. It was a let-off for United and potentially a big moment in a difficult season for Lammens.

But he undid his good work 75 seconds later when Maxi Araujo chased a long ball over the top pursued by Noussair Mazraoui. For some reason, Lammens thought it would be a good idea to race 25 yards out of his goal.

Araujo stepped inside the Belgium goalkeeper and went down under his clumsy challenge. Marciniak pointed to the spot again, and this time Suarez made no mistake.

Lammens started positively saving this Luis Suarez penalty before conceding a spot-kick

Yet, minutes later Suarez scored after being given a second penalty following Lammens error

United thought they had eqaulised before half-time but Amad Diallo's header was ruled out for a percieved foul in the build-up by Youri Tielemans that earned him a booking

After all the upset over the officiating at Anfield, United were on the wrong end of another big call just before half-time here when Tielemans stretched to poke the ball through to Diallo and inadvertently caught Goncalo Inacio who went down claiming serious injury.

Goalkeeper Kaique Pereira saved Diallo's first effort and Marciniak blew his whistle for a foul before the Ivorian headed in at the second attempt so there was no opportunity for VAR to review it. The referee booked Tielemans, but there was a strong argument that it wasn't even a foul.

United re-emerged for the second half undeterred and hit back to score twice through Fernandes within five minutes of the restart.

The United captain played the ball through for Martinez and then converted from the spot after his team-mate went down in a tangle of legs with Eduardo Quaresma.

Bruno Fernandes levelled for United just after half-time when they were awarded a penalty

He then put them ahead with this left-footed shot that hit a divot on the pitch before flying in

United's lead was undone late on when Lammens' second major error allowed Suarez to score

United's evening was compounded when Tielemans was sent off late on for a second yellow

Two minutes later, and having made the divot turning in the penalty box 17 seconds earlier, Fernandes somehow managed to hit it with a hopeful effort from 25 yards. Pereira had the ball covered but it took an outrageous deflection just outside the six-yard box and flew through his arms.

But this is United and nothing is straightforward. In the 80th minute, with victory within their grasp, Lammens had all the time in the world to catch a high ball from Ivan Fresneda. Perhaps too long. Unforgivably, he dropped it in front of Suarez who hooked into the net.

There was still time for more drama when United had another goal from a Fernandes' corner chalked off for Patrick Dorgu's foul on Pereira, after VAR sent Marciniak to the monitor, and he then showed Tielemans a second yellow card.

Pochettino looked on frustrated and probably as confused as the rest of us.

#1286. Narrow Defeat For Under-21s In Final Trophy Game

Everton Under-21s' Jersey Mikes Trophy campaign ended with a third straight group stage defeat at the hands of Tranmere Rovers.

The Prenton Park tie was a dead rubber with Everton already eliminated and Rovers already through to the knockout stage.

Charlie Veevers created an early opening for the home side on the left edge of the Everton box but his shot was deflected wide for a corner.

The Blues' first opening came after a quarter of an hour. Rovers midfielder Sam Finley played a sloppy pass straight to Malik Olayiwola but the final effort from distance was blocked.

Everton took the lead five minutes later when Olayiwola played in Braiden Graham who was sharp enough to get to the ball before Coniah Boyce-Clarke and poke it into the net.

There was a chance for Tranmere to hit back quickly but Veevers and David Kamara contrived to get in each other's way inside the Everton penalty area and the former lashed his shot well wide of the target. Shortly after, Olayiwola’s flick provided Graham with another sight of goal but this time the best he could do was win a corner.

The hosts levelled just before the break when Kamara timed his forward run well enough to just stay onside before steering a neat finish past Fraser Barnsley.

There was a touch of good fortune to the goal that gave Rovers the lead early in the second half and ultimately secured the victory. Veevers' effort would probably have been covered by Barnsley had it not taken a nick off Will Tamen on the way.

Kamara tested Barnsley from a narrow angle on 62 minutes and from the subsequent corner kick Ryan Watson headed over, and at the other end Melvin Matos was desperately unfortunate to see his superbly struck shot strike the Rovers crossbar.

To their credit, Everton stuck at it and kept themselves in the game. Olayiwola was next to try his luck but from distance he thumped the ball high over the bar.

Two Everton substitutes combined well with 10 minutes remaining. Shea Pita played a beautifully weighted pass into the path of George Finney who surprised Boyce-Clarke with a first-time shot that the keeper gathered at the second attempt.

Boyce-Clarke had to be alert again in added time to keep out a snapshot volley from Matos.

Speaking after the game, Head of Academy Player Development Dave Hughes told evertonfc.com: "If you look at the first half performance, we thought we were worthy of being a goal up. The progress from the first (Jersey Mikes Trophy) game at Stockport to tonight is clear in terms of more maturity and better decision-making in the way they try to play.

"Towards the end of the game we were still pushing forward and trying to get an equaliser but the reality of it is for the boys to get to where they want to be, they’ve got to find a way to win.

"We looked composed with the ball and we were on the front foot but at the end of the game experience showed and they managed the critical moments better, which is where we’ve got to improve and we’ll keep nursing the lads along.

"(In) the first 15 minutes of the second half they came at us quite quickly and we switch off from a throw-in which leads to a goal, but we feel that we are making progress. Harvey Foster was excellent in the first half, Will Tamen was outstanding and there were some really good performances so we’re really pleased.

"Melvin Matos is relentless. He’s got this unbelievable knack of pressing the life out of people and closing the space very quickly. If he can get his first touch out of his feet and run at the backline, he’s a threat.

"He’s developing nicely. He’s got plenty of work still to do but with all the guys their appetite to work and seek improvement and develop has been outstanding.

"We tell them that if you want a career in the game then winning is essential and you need the mentality to keep improving your performance. Within that as individuals you have to show grit and steel and play with character and personality."
